When somebody attacks your position in public, your instinct is to defend it immediately. Resist that for five seconds. The most powerful move in a hostile exchange is to restate the other person's argument so fairly that they say, yes, exactly. It does three things. It shows the room you were listening. It forces the other person to agree with you about what the disagreement actually is. And it gives you time to think. Only then should you concede what is true, and there is almost always something true. After that, push back on the one point that matters, and turn it into a hypothesis the room can discuss. People can argue with a hypothesis for an hour without anybody losing face. They cannot do that with an accusation.

Thank you, David, and I am going to stop you there, because I want to make sure the room has your main point before we lose it. If I understand you correctly, what you are saying is that the auction calendar, not the tariff, is what keeps investors away. Is that fair? Good. Now, that is a claim the fund side will want to test, so let me bring in Maria. Maria, you have been shaking your head for two minutes. Should the calendar be fixed by law, as David suggests, would your fund bid in the first round, or would you still wait? And a caveat for everyone: we have eleven minutes left, so I will ask you to keep your answers under ninety seconds.

The first thing I tell people is that the audience is not scoring your answer. They are scoring your face while you decide what to say. That half second before you open your mouth carries more information than the sentence that follows it. So the drill is not about clever phrases. It is about the pause. You take the question, you let one full beat go by, and then you speak. It feels endless from the inside. From the outside it reads as somebody who is thinking rather than reciting. Now, the content. There are three honest moves and everybody forgets two of them. You can answer it. You can say why you are not going to answer it. Or you can say you do not know and tell the room when you will. What people do instead is a fourth thing, which is to answer a neighbouring question and hope nobody noticed. They always notice. I also make people write down their red lines before the event. Not vague ones. The specific numbers and names they will not give, in writing, the night before. It sounds bureaucratic and it is the single most useful thing on the list, because once you know exactly what you are protecting, you stop protecting everything. That is the difference between an executive who sounds open and one who sounds like a press release. And when it gets hot, slow down. Everybody speeds up. The person who slows down owns the room.
